conventions.convention: The Fourier transform is the negative-sign, 2-pi-normalized integral f-hat(xi) = integral f(x) exp(-2 pi i x.xi) dx on L1 classes, and the output is a function defined at every frequency, not an almost-everywhere class; at frequency zero it reads integral f.

Inversion uses the positive-sign integral g(x) = integral f-hat(xi) exp(+2 pi i x.xi) dxi; the L1 inversion conclusions are almost-everywhere equality plus equality at each specified Lebesgue value, never equality for an arbitrary representative at every point.

Schwartz space consists of actual smooth functions (not equivalence classes) with seminorms p_{alpha beta}(f) = sup over R^n of |x^alpha partial^beta f(x)|, for n >= 1; the family separates functions.

Schwartz convergence is convergence in every seminorm p_{alpha beta}; this pair defines local convexity of a complex TVS as zero admitting a base of convex balanced sets (weaker-looking than the companion page's 'every zero-neighbourhood contains a convex one', but equivalent given the scalar-continuity verifications in the item).

A topological vector space has jointly continuous addition on X x X and scalar multiplication on K x X; a zero-neighbourhood need not be open; Hausdorffness, local convexity and any choice principle are separate hypotheses, and the zero vector space with its unique topology is allowed.

Local convexity means every zero-neighbourhood contains a convex zero-neighbourhood (equivalently there is a base of open convex zero-neighbourhoods); convexity always uses real coefficients, even over C; balanced means |lambda| <= 1 implies lambda C subset C; the continuous dual X' is the space of continuous K-linear functionals and separation inequalities are stated for Re f.

The Minkowski gauge of an open convex zero-neighbourhood is p_U(x) = inf{t > 0 : x in tU}, a finite real infimum over positive reals; no symmetry, balance or positive definiteness is built in, and U = {p_U < 1} uses openness of U.

The three separation theorems explicitly assume HB, the real dominated-extension principle over ZF (not AC and not a theorem of ZF), and state their conclusions for the real part; over C the real functional is converted by f(x) = H(x) - i H(ix).

Items on these pages that use the Euclidean measure, integral or approximation interfaces carry an explicit 'Assume countable choice' hypothesis in their statements (translation continuity, convolution, Fubini/Tonelli, Plancherel, Schwartz integrability, Poisson summation and the Lebesgue-point machinery).

The two measure-smoothing/uniqueness items assume the full Axiom of Choice (Radon-Nikodym existence, Hahn/Jordan selections), while the transform of a finite complex measure itself only assumes countable choice; this AC assumption must be retained by consumers of measure uniqueness.

Gaussian summability normalization: k_t(x) = t^{-n/2} exp(-pi|x|^2/t), k-hat_t(xi) = exp(-pi t|xi|^2), S_t f = f * k_t; the radial profile used in the Lebesgue-point lemma is K(y) = exp(-pi|y|^2), Phi(r) = exp(-pi r^2) with epsilon = sqrt(t).

A Lebesgue value at x with value a is the oscillation condition A(r) = integral over |y| < r of |f(x-y) - a| dy = o(r^n); all pointwise inversion and summability conclusions are pinned to this specified value, not to an arbitrary changed representative value.

Plancherel is the unique norm-preserving extension of the Schwartz transform to L2 preserving the first-variable-linear pairing <f,g> = integral f conj(g); the integral transform and the L2 transform agree only on L1 intersect L2 (almost everywhere), and L2 inversion is norm convergence of truncated integrals, with no pointwise assertion.

Schwartz Fourier calculus: F(partial^alpha f)(xi) = (2 pi i xi)^alpha f-hat(xi) and partial^beta f-hat = F((-2 pi i x)^beta f); on Schwartz space F^2 = R and F is a topological automorphism, with inversion holding at every point.

Real L2 multipliers: D(M) = {f in H : mf in H} for finite real measurable m, adjoint defined by <Mf,g> = <f,h> for every f in D(M); the transported exponential e^{itP} = U^{-1}V_tU is only that explicit object, with norm-derivative iP defined exactly on D(P) = U^{-1}D(M) -- no abstract spectral theorem.

Heisenberg inequality with the exact constant n/(4 pi) times ||f||_2^2; for nonzero f equality holds exactly for f(x) = c exp(-lambda|x-a|^2/2) exp(2 pi i b.x) with c nonzero, lambda > 0, and the zero function also gives equality.

load_bearing.statement: A topological vector space is a K-vector space with a topology for which addition on X x X and scalar multiplication on K x X are jointly continuous; a Hausdorff TVS additionally has disjoint open neighbourhoods for distinct points; Hausdorffness is a separate hypothesis, and no norm, metric, local convexity or choice assumption is included.

Convex sets and hulls, balanced and absolutely convex sets, local convexity as a convex (equivalently open convex) zero-neighbourhood base, seminorms, and the continuous dual X' of continuous K-linear functionals; for separation inequalities one writes u = Re f, and no Hahn-Banach or choice principle is part of the definitions.

Translations and multiplication by a nonzero scalar are homeomorphisms; every zero-neighbourhood U absorbs every x; there is a symmetric open zero-neighbourhood W with W+W subset U; every scalar-linear functional bounded in modulus on a zero-neighbourhood is continuous; scalar addition and multiplication are jointly continuous.

Assume HB. Let A, B be nonempty disjoint convex subsets of a real or complex TVS X, and suppose A is open. There are a nonzero continuous K-linear functional f and alpha in R such that Re f(a) < alpha <= Re f(b) for all a in A, b in B; if B is also open, the same alpha may be chosen with both inequalities strict.

f-hat(xi) = F f(xi) := integral over R^n of f(x) exp(-2 pi i x.xi) dx for f in L1(R^n;C); the output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class, and no choice selection of representatives is part of the definition.
The map F: L1(R^n;C) -> BUC(R^n;C) is complex-linear and sup over xi of |f-hat(xi)| <= ||f||_1 (BUC = bounded uniformly continuous functions).
Assume countable choice. For n >= 1, t > 0 and xi in R^n: F(exp(-pi t|x|^2))(xi) = t^{-n/2} exp(-pi|xi|^2/t); every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, 2 pi-normalized Fourier transform is continuous from Schwartz space to itself, and F(partial^alpha f)(xi) = (2 pi i xi)^alpha f-hat(xi), partial^beta f-hat = F((-2 pi i x)^beta f).

Assume countable choice. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry F_2: L2(R^n;C) -> L2(R^n;C); it preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume countable choice. If f in L1(R^n;C) and f-hat is in L1, then g(x) = integral f-hat(xi) exp(2 pi i x.xi) dxi is bounded and continuous, equals f almost everywhere, and equals the specified value at every Lebesgue point of f.

Assume countable choice. For complex C1 functions u, v on [a,b], integral u'v = u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) - integral u v'; if u, v are C1 on R with u'v, u v' in L1 and u(x)v(x) -> 0 as x -> +-infinity, then integral u'v = -integral u v'.

Assume countable choice. If f is in Schwartz space, then x^alpha partial^beta f is in Lp for every 1 <= p <= infinity and every pair of multi-indices, with norm bounded by a finite sum of Schwartz seminorms.

p_{alpha beta}(f) = sup over x in R^n of |x^alpha partial^beta f(x)|, and Schwartz space is the set of smooth complex functions with all p_{alpha beta}(f) finite; these are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes, and the seminorms separate functions.

concerns.concern: The uniform-continuity proof compresses two reconstructions into one sentence: it obtains a single delta from 'continuity of the exponential at zero' on the compact ball |x| <= R (a Heine-Cantor/finite-subcover step that is not written), and it selects an integer R with integral over |x| > R of |f| < epsilon/4 via dominated convergence. I could not find any step requiring countable choice (the library's dominated convergence is choice-free and the compactness step is finite), so this looks like an unstated convention rather than a gap, but the statement records no choice convention while the page prose promises that items using the Euclidean approximation interfaces state countable choice. A judge should confirm the one-line reconstructions and the choice-free reading.

The proof says countable choice 'also covers the near-maximizing partition selections in the imported total-variation additivity proof', but does not name the item or the exact step; the item's own two proof steps (a bounded integral against a finite measure and dominated convergence) are choice-free. The near-maximizing partition selection I could locate is in thm-total-variation-is-the-supremum-of-unit-bounded-simple-integrals, step 1.2, and the explicit choice of approximating simple functions is in def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure, so the attribution is plausible but its locator is imprecise.

The 'Given' paragraph cites def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn as 'the test convention', but that item defines real-valued C_c/C_c-infinity spaces while the statement quantifies over complex test functions phi in C_c(R^n); the complex convention is fixed by def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions (componentwise complexification), which the item does not cite directly. Also, the extension of 'integral H dmu = integral Hu dv' from simple to bounded measurable H is described only as 'quantizing its real and imaginary values'.

This item defines local convexity of a complex TVS as 'zero has a base of convex balanced sets', whereas the companion batch-2 page defines local convexity as 'every zero-neighbourhood contains a convex zero-neighbourhood (equivalently a base of open convex zero-neighbourhoods)'. For the seminorm topology at hand both hold, and the item verifies the TVS axioms, but the two wordings differ and a cross-reading judge should confirm the intended equivalence is not doing extra work here (the bridging argument is lem-balanced-convex-zero-neighborhood-refinement on the other page).
